code.title: Depth (passed down) and height (returned up)

followUps:
A tree with one node has height 1 if you count nodes and height 0 if you count edges.

The longest path from the root down to a leaf is just the root itself: that is one node and zero edges. This follows from the base case: with height(null) = 0 you get 1 + max(0, 0) = 1, and with height(null) = -1 you get 1 + max(-1, -1) = 0. The two conventions always differ by exactly 1, so say which one you use before you write code.

It asks for the height of the root, counted in nodes: the number of nodes on the longest path from the root to a leaf.

The name says "depth" because the deepest leaf sits at that depth, but the number you return is the root's height. For the tree 3 -> (9, 20 -> (15, 7)) the longest path is 3, 20, 15, so the answer is 3. An empty tree gives 0 and a single node gives 1.

int maxDepth(Node n) {
  if (n == null) return 0;
  return 1 + Math.max(maxDepth(n.left), maxDepth(n.right));
}

Time O(N), space O(h).

code.title: Preorder, inorder and postorder on one tree

followUps:
Postorder gives Reverse Polish Notation, because it writes both operands before the operator that joins them.

Take (3 + 4) * 5. The tree has * at the root, + as its left child (with leaves 3 and 4) and 5 as its right child. Postorder visits left, right, then the node: 3 4 + 5 *. A stack machine can run that directly: push 3, push 4, add to get 7, push 5, multiply to get 35. Preorder gives prefix (Polish) notation * + 3 4 5, and inorder gives the usual infix form but needs brackets. Time O(N), space O(h).

No, a single plain traversal is not enough in general, because many different shapes produce the same list.

Preorder 1 2 fits two trees: 2 as the left child of 1, or 2 as the right child of 1. Inorder 1 2 is just as unclear. You need more information:

  • inorder plus preorder (or inorder plus postorder), with all values different;
  • one traversal that also writes a marker for every empty child, such as 1,2,#,#,#;
  • preorder alone if you know the tree is a BST, because sorting it gives you the inorder.

code.title: Inorder traversal with an explicit stack
code.python:
class Node:
    def __init__(self, val, left=None, right=None):
        self.val, self.left, self.right = val, left, right

root = Node(4, Node(2, Node(1), Node(3)), Node(6, Node(5), Node(7)))
print("BST: 4 -> (2 -> (1, 3), 6 -> (5, 7))")
stack = []
out = []
cur = root
max_stack = 0
while cur is not None or stack:
    # Slide left, remembering every node we still owe a visit.
    while cur is not None:
        stack.append(cur)
        cur = cur.left
    max_stack = max(max_stack, len(stack))
    # The top of the stack has its whole left side done: record it.
    n = stack.pop()
    out.append(str(n.val))
    # Then handle its right subtree the same way.
    cur = n.right
print("inorder: " + " ".join(out))
print("largest stack size:", max_stack)
# Time O(N): each node is pushed and popped once. Space O(h).

followUps:
Yes: keep one stack plus a pointer last to the node you recorded most recently, and record a node only when its right side is empty or already done.

  1. Slide left, pushing nodes.
  2. Peek at the top. If it has a right child that is not last, go into that right child.
  3. Otherwise record the top, pop it and remember it as last.
while (cur != null || !st.isEmpty()) {
  if (cur != null) { st.push(cur); cur = cur.left; continue; }
  Node top = st.peek();
  if (top.right != null && top.right != last) cur = top.right;
  else { visit(top); last = st.pop(); }
}

For 1 -> (2, 3) it records 2, 3, 1. Time O(N), space O(h).

Yes. Morris traversal uses no stack: it borrows the empty right pointer of a node's inorder predecessor as a temporary link back up.

At cur: if there is no left child, record it and go right. Otherwise find the rightmost node of the left subtree. If its right pointer is empty, point it at cur and go left. If it already points at cur, the left side is finished: remove the link, record cur, go right.

if (cur.left == null) { visit(cur); cur = cur.right; continue; }
Node p = cur.left;
while (p.right != null && p.right != cur) p = p.right;
if (p.right == null) { p.right = cur; cur = cur.left; }
else { p.right = null; visit(cur); cur = cur.right; }

Time O(N), extra space O(1). The tree is changed during the walk and restored at the end, so it is unsafe if other threads read it.

code.title: BFS level by level, nearest leaf, and DFS maximum depth
code.python:
from collections import deque

class Node:
    def __init__(self, val, left=None, right=None):
        self.val, self.left, self.right = val, left, right

def max_depth(n):   # DFS: a whole-subtree question
    return 0 if n is None else 1 + max(max_depth(n.left), max_depth(n.right))

root = Node(1, Node(2, Node(4, Node(7)), Node(5)), Node(3))
print("Tree: 1 -> (2 -> (4 -> (7), 5), 3)")
queue = deque([root])
level = 0
leaf_val = leaf_depth = -1
while queue:
    size = len(queue)   # how many nodes are on this level
    line = []
    for _ in range(size):
        n = queue.popleft()
        line.append(str(n.val))
        # The first leaf BFS meets is the nearest one.
        if leaf_depth < 0 and n.left is None and n.right is None:
            leaf_val, leaf_depth = n.val, level + 1
        if n.left: queue.append(n.left)
        if n.right: queue.append(n.right)
    print("level " + str(level) + ": " + " ".join(line))
    level += 1
print("BFS: nearest leaf is", leaf_val, "at depth", leaf_depth, "(counting nodes)")
print("DFS: maximum depth =", max_depth(root))
# Both are O(N) time. BFS space O(widest level), DFS space O(h).

followUps:
DFS uses far less: about 20 stack entries, against roughly half a million queue entries for BFS.

A perfect tree with 220 - 1 = 1,048,575 nodes has 20 levels. DFS only keeps the path from the root to the current node, so at most 20 frames. BFS keeps a whole level in the queue, and the last level alone has 219 = 524,288 nodes. So on a wide, balanced tree DFS is O(log N) memory and BFS is O(N). On a skewed tree (a chain) it flips: BFS holds 1 node at a time while DFS holds all N.

Pass the depth down as a parameter and put each value into the list that belongs to its depth.

  1. Keep a list of lists, levels.
  2. When you reach a depth for the first time, add a new empty list.
  3. Add the node's value to levels[depth], then go left before right so each level stays in left-to-right order.
void dfs(Node n, int depth, List<List<Integer>> levels) {
  if (n == null) return;
  if (depth == levels.size()) levels.add(new ArrayList<>());
  levels.get(depth).add(n.val);
  dfs(n.left, depth + 1, levels);
  dfs(n.right, depth + 1, levels);
}

For 1 -> (2 -> (4), 3) it builds [[1], [2, 3], [4]]. Time O(N), space O(h) besides the output.

code.title: Diameter in one postorder pass
code.python:
class Node:
    def __init__(self, val, left=None, right=None):
        self.val, self.left, self.right = val, left, right

best = 0

# Returns the height in nodes (what the parent needs) and
# records the longest path that bends at this node (what we want).
def height(n):
    global best
    if n is None:
        return 0
    lh, rh = height(n.left), height(n.right)
    best = max(best, lh + rh)   # edges on the path through n
    return 1 + max(lh, rh)      # a parent can use one side only

left = Node(2, Node(4, Node(6, Node(8))), Node(5, Node(7, Node(9))))
root = Node(1, left, Node(3))
print("Tree: 1 -> (2 -> (4 -> (6 -> (8)), 5 -> (7 -> (9))), 3)")
height(root)
print("diameter =", best, "edges (path 8-6-4-2-5-7-9, bending at node 2)")
via_root = height(root.left) + height(root.right)
print("longest path through the root =", via_root, "edges")
# Time O(N): one visit per node. Space O(h) for the recursion stack.

followUps:
No. The longest path can sit completely inside one subtree and never touch the root.

Picture a root 1 whose right child is the single node 3, and whose left child 2 has two long arms: 2-4-6-8 and 2-5-7-9. The path 8-6-4-2-5-7-9 has 6 edges and bends at node 2. The best path through the root is 3-1-2-4-6-8 with only 5 edges. That is why the code checks leftHeight + rightHeight at every node and keeps the largest value, instead of computing it once at the root.

Use two breadth-first searches: go from any node to the farthest node A, then from A to the farthest node B. The distance from A to B is the diameter.

  1. Build an adjacency list from the edge list.
  2. BFS from node 0 and take the last node reached, A. It is always one end of a longest path.
  3. BFS from A; the largest distance found is the diameter.

Example with edges 1-2, 2-3, 3-4, 2-5: BFS from 1 ends at 4 (distance 3). BFS from 4 reaches 1 and 5 at distance 3, so the diameter is 3 edges. Time O(N), space O(N). A DFS that keeps the two tallest child heights at each node also works.

code.title: Balanced check that returns height or -1

followUps:
Because an AVL tree of height h must contain a number of nodes that grows exponentially with h, so N nodes can only reach a height of about 1.44 log2 N.

Let m(h) be the fewest nodes an AVL tree of height h can have. The thinnest such tree has one subtree of height h - 1 and one of height h - 2 (they may differ by 1), so m(h) = m(h - 1) + m(h - 2) + 1. That gives 1, 2, 4, 7, 12, 20, 33 for heights 1 to 7, which grows like the Fibonacci numbers, about 1.618h. Turn it around: a tree with 1,000,000 nodes cannot be taller than about 28 levels, so every search, insert and delete is O(log N).

The simplest way is to read the keys out in sorted order and rebuild the tree from the middle outwards.

  1. Do an inorder walk and store the nodes in an array; a BST gives them sorted.
  2. Pick the middle element as the root, build the left half as its left subtree and the right half as its right subtree, recursively.
Node build(List<Node> a, int lo, int hi) {
  if (lo > hi) return null;
  int mid = (lo + hi) / 2; Node n = a.get(mid);
  n.left = build(a, lo, mid - 1); n.right = build(a, mid + 1, hi);
  return n;
}

Keys 1..7 inserted in order form a chain of height 7; rebuilt, 4 becomes the root and the height is 3. Time O(N), space O(N). The Day-Stout-Warren method does the same with rotations in O(1) extra space.

code.title: Lowest common ancestor: binary-tree method and BST method

followUps:
Then the usual shortcut is wrong, so count how many of the two targets you really found and return an answer only when the count is 2.

The standard code returns as soon as it meets p, without looking below it. If q is missing, it still returns p as the "LCA". Fix: always search both children first (true postorder), add 1 to a counter each time a target is seen, and check the counter at the end.

Node l = find(n.left, p, q), r = find(n.right, p, q);
if (n == p || n == q) { found++; return n; }
if (l != null && r != null) return n;
return l != null ? l : r;
// caller: Node ans = find(root, p, q); return found == 2 ? ans : null;

Example: in 1 -> (2, 3), asking for 2 and 9 gives found = 1, so the answer is null instead of 2. Still O(N) time and O(h) space, but with no early exit.

Add the two depths and subtract twice the depth of the LCA: dist(p, q) = depth(p) + depth(q) - 2 * depth(lca).

The path from p to q climbs from p up to the LCA and then goes down to q. Each depth counts the edges from the root, and both counts include the shared piece from the root to the LCA, so that piece is removed twice. Example in the tree 6 -> (2 -> (0, 4 -> (3, 5)), 8 -> (7, 9)): depth(3) = 3, depth(7) = 2, LCA is 6 at depth 0, so the distance is 3 + 2 - 0 = 5 edges (3-4-2-6-8-7). For 3 and 0: 3 + 2 - 2*1 = 3 edges. One LCA search plus two depth searches is O(N) time, O(h) space.

code.title: BST delete: leaf, one child, two children

followUps:
Because the successor is the leftmost node of the right subtree, and "leftmost" means we stopped only when there was no left child left to follow.

To find it we step right once and then keep going left while a left child exists. If the node we stopped at had a left child, that child would be smaller, still inside the right subtree, and the loop would have moved on to it. Example: delete 50 from 50 -> (30, 70 -> (60 -> (null, 65), 80)). Go right to 70, left to 60, stop: 60 has no left child. It may have a right child (65), so removing 60 is the leaf case or the one-child case, never the two-child case again.

The search and the three delete cases stay the same; what is added is repair work on the way back up so the tree stays balanced.

  • AVL tree: after the removal, every node on the path back to the root updates its stored height. If the two sides now differ by 2, a single or double rotation fixes it. A delete may need a rotation at several levels, up to O(log N) of them.
  • Red-black tree: removing a black node breaks the "same number of black nodes on every path" rule. It is repaired with recolouring and at most 3 rotations.

Example: an AVL tree 2 -> (1, 3 -> (null, 4)); delete 1 and node 2 has heights 0 and 2, so one left rotation makes 3 the root. The total cost stays O(log N), and now that is guaranteed.

code.title: Validate a BST: children-only bug versus range check

followUps:
It follows from one fact: for any node X, inorder lists everything in X's left subtree before X and everything in X's right subtree after X.

Take any node X. By the Left, Node, Right rule, all nodes of its left subtree appear earlier in the list than X, and all nodes of its right subtree appear later. If the list is strictly increasing, everything earlier is smaller and everything later is larger. So every value in X's left subtree is less than X and every value in its right subtree is greater. X was any node, so this holds everywhere, which is exactly the definition of a BST.

Check with 5 -> (1, 6 -> (3, 7)): inorder is 1 5 3 6 7. The drop from 5 to 3 shows that 3, which is in 5's right subtree, is smaller than 5.

Use one postorder pass where every subtree reports three things to its parent: its size if it is a BST (or -1 if it is not), its smallest value and its largest value.

A node forms a BST when both children do, and max(left) < node < min(right). An empty subtree reports size 0, min = +infinity, max = -infinity so the test passes.

int[] l = go(n.left), r = go(n.right);   // {size, min, max}
if (l[0] < 0 || r[0] < 0 || l[2] >= n.val || n.val >= r[1])
  return new int[]{-1, 0, 0};
int size = l[0] + r[0] + 1;  best = Math.max(best, size);
return new int[]{size, Math.min(l[1], n.val), Math.max(r[2], n.val)};

For 10 -> (5 -> (1, 8), 15 -> (null, 7)): the subtree at 5 is a BST of size 3; at 15 the right child 7 is too small; so the answer is 3. Time O(N), space O(h).

code.title: K-th smallest in a BST: inorder walk and subtree sizes

followUps:
Walk down from the root towards x, and every time you step right, add the size of the left subtree you skipped plus 1 for the node itself.

Those are exactly the keys that are smaller than x. Stepping left adds nothing, because that node and its right side are all larger.

int rank = 0;                       // keys smaller than x
while (n != null) {
  if (x <= n.val) n = n.left;
  else { rank += size(n.left) + 1; n = n.right; }
}
return rank + 1;                    // 1-based position of x

Tree 5 -> (3 -> (1, 4), 8 -> (7, 9)), x = 8: at 5 go right and add 3 + 1 = 4; at 8 go left; at 7 go right and add 0 + 1; rank = 5, so 8 is the 6th smallest. Time O(h), space O(1).

Keep a max-heap that holds only the k smallest values seen so far; its top is the k-th smallest at every moment.

  1. Push each new value.
  2. If the heap now has more than k items, pop the largest.
  3. The top of the heap is the current answer.
PriorityQueue<Integer> heap = new PriorityQueue<>(Collections.reverseOrder());
for (int x : stream) {
  heap.add(x);
  if (heap.size() > k) heap.poll();
}
return heap.peek();

Stream 7, 2, 9, 4, 1 with k = 3: the heap goes {7}, {7,2}, {9,7,2}, then 4 pushes out 9, then 1 pushes out 7, leaving {4,2,1}; the answer is 4. Time O(N log k), space O(k). It only supports adding values; if values can also be removed you need the size-augmented balanced tree.

code.title: Build a tree from preorder and inorder in O(N)
code.python:
class Node:
    def __init__(self, val):
        self.val, self.left, self.right = val, None, None

pre = [3, 9, 20, 15, 7]
ino = [9, 3, 15, 20, 7]
pos = {v: i for i, v in enumerate(ino)}   # value -> index in inorder
nxt = 0                                   # next unused preorder index

# Builds the subtree whose values are ino[lo..hi].
def build(lo, hi):
    global nxt
    if lo > hi:
        return None
    root = Node(pre[nxt])          # the next preorder value is this subtree's root
    nxt += 1
    m = pos[root.val]              # O(1) lookup of where it splits inorder
    root.left = build(lo, m - 1)   # left first: preorder lists the left subtree next
    root.right = build(m + 1, hi)
    return root

def postorder(n, out):
    if n is None:
        return
    postorder(n.left, out)
    postorder(n.right, out)
    out.append(str(n.val))

root = build(0, len(ino) - 1)
out = []
postorder(root, out)
print("preorder: 3 9 20 15 7")
print("inorder: 9 3 15 20 7")
print("root = " + str(root.val) + ", left child = " + str(root.left.val) + ", right child = " + str(root.right.val))
print("postorder of built tree: " + " ".join(out))
# Time O(N): one node and one map lookup per value. Space O(N) for the map.

followUps:
Because preorder and postorder together cannot tell you whether an only child is a left child or a right child, so several trees fit the same pair.

Smallest example: preorder 1 2 and postorder 2 1. The tree "2 is the left child of 1" gives these lists, and so does "2 is the right child of 1". Inorder is what separates them (2 1 versus 1 2), because it places the root between its two sides. The pair preorder + postorder is unique only when every node has 0 or 2 children (a full binary tree); for other trees you can build one valid tree, but not know it is the original.

Read the preorder left to right and give each recursive call an upper bound: a value belongs to the current subtree only if it is smaller than that bound.

No inorder is needed, because a BST's inorder is just the sorted values. Keep one shared index i.

Node build(int[] pre, long bound) {
  if (i == pre.length || pre[i] > bound) return null;
  Node n = new Node(pre[i++]);
  n.left = build(pre, n.val);     // left side: everything below n
  n.right = build(pre, bound);    // right side: up to the parent's bound
  return n; }

For [8, 5, 1, 7, 10, 12] called with bound = infinity: 8 is the root; 5, 1, 7 are below 8 and form the left side; 10 is above 8, so the left call returns and 10, 12 form the right side. Each value is consumed once, so time is O(N) and space is O(h).

code.title: Plain BST height: sorted inserts versus middle-first inserts
code.python:
class Node:
    def __init__(self, val):
        self.val, self.left, self.right = val, None, None

root = None
height = 0   # deepest level reached so far, counting nodes

# Plain BST insert with a loop (no balancing). Cost = depth of the new node.
def insert(key):
    global root, height
    depth = 1
    if root is None:
        root = Node(key)
    else:
        n = root
        while True:
            depth += 1
            if key < n.val:
                if n.left is None:
                    n.left = Node(key)
                    break
                n = n.left
            else:
                if n.right is None:
                    n.right = Node(key)
                    break
                n = n.right
    height = max(height, depth)

# Insert the middle key first, then the middles of each half: a balanced shape.
def insert_middle_first(lo, hi):
    if lo > hi:
        return
    mid = (lo + hi) // 2
    insert(mid)
    insert_middle_first(lo, mid - 1)
    insert_middle_first(mid + 1, hi)

n = 1000
for k in range(1, n + 1):   # sorted keys: every key goes right
    insert(k)
print("Insert 1.." + str(n) + " in sorted order: height =", height)
root, height = None, 0
insert_middle_first(1, n)
print("Insert the same keys middle-first: height =", height)
print("A red-black tree keeps the height near log2(N) for any insert order")
# Search costs O(height): O(N) for the chain, O(log N) when balanced.

followUps:
Choose a hash map when you only look keys up by their exact value and never need them in order.

A hash map does get, put and remove in O(1) on average; an ordered map needs O(log N). With 1,000,000 keys that is about 1 hash computation against about 20 comparisons. Choose the ordered map when you need any of these, which a hash map cannot do without scanning everything:

  • keys in sorted order;
  • the smallest or largest key;
  • the nearest key below or above a value (floor, ceiling);
  • all keys in a range, such as times between 9:00 and 10:00.

The ordered map also has a guaranteed O(log N) worst case, while a hash map can slow down when many keys collide.

A rotation is a small local change of three pointers that lifts a child above its parent, making one side of the tree shorter and the other taller.

Right rotation at y, whose left child is x: x moves up into y's place, y becomes x's right child, and x's old right subtree (call it B) becomes y's left subtree.

Node rotateRight(Node y) {
  Node x = y.left;
  y.left = x.right;   // B moves across
  x.right = y;
  return x;           // new top of this subtree
}

Order is kept because inorder before and after is the same: A, x, B, y, C. B holds keys between x and y, and it is still to the right of x and to the left of y. Example: 3 -> (2 -> (1)) becomes 2 -> (1, 3); inorder is 1 2 3 both times and the height drops from 3 to 2. Cost O(1).

code.title: Serialize and deserialize a tree with duplicate values
code.python:
class Node:
    def __init__(self, val, left=None, right=None):
        self.val, self.left, self.right = val, left, right

# Preorder, writing "#" for every empty child so the shape is recorded.
def encode(n, out):
    if n is None:
        out.append("#")
        return
    out.append(str(n.val))
    encode(n.left, out)
    encode(n.right, out)

def serialize(root):
    out = []
    encode(root, out)
    return ",".join(out)

# Mirrors encode: read one token, then a whole left subtree, then a right one.
def deserialize(s):
    tokens = iter(s.split(","))
    def decode():
        t = next(tokens)
        if t == "#":
            return None
        n = Node(int(t))
        n.left = decode()
        n.right = decode()
        return n
    return decode()

root = Node(1, Node(2), Node(2, Node(4), Node(2)))
print("Tree with duplicates: 1 -> (2, 2 -> (4, 2))")
s = serialize(root)
print("serialized: " + s)
copy = deserialize(s)
again = serialize(copy)
print("decoded and serialized again: " + again)
print("round trip matches: " + ("yes" if s == again else "no"))
# Both directions: O(N) time, O(N) space for the tokens, O(h) recursion.

followUps:
Write each node as its value followed by the number of children it has, then write the children one after another in the same way.

A node can have any number of children, so "left" and "right" markers no longer work; the child count tells the decoder how many subtrees to read next.

void encode(Node n, StringBuilder sb) {
  sb.append(n.val).append(' ').append(n.children.size()).append(' ');
  for (Node c : n.children) encode(c, sb);
}

Tree 1 -> (3 -> (5, 6), 2, 4) becomes 1 3 3 2 5 0 6 0 2 0 4 0: node 1 has 3 children, node 3 has 2, and the rest have 0. The decoder reads a value and a count k, then calls itself k times. Another option is an "end of children" marker after each child list. Both ways are O(N) time and space.

Yes. For a BST with distinct keys the preorder list alone is enough, because the ordering rule tells the decoder where every value must go.

Write plain preorder with no markers. To decode, read the values left to right and pass an upper bound down: a value is placed in the current subtree only if it is below the bound, otherwise the call returns and an ancestor takes it. Example: 5,3,1,4,8. 5 is the root; 3, 1 and 4 are below 5, so they form the left side (1 left of 3, 4 right of 3); 8 is above 5, so it becomes the right child. That saves the N + 1 null markers, about half of the output. Decoding is O(N). With duplicates you must first fix a rule, such as "equal keys always go right".

code.title: Height of a 100000-node skewed tree with an explicit stack
code.python:
class Node:
    def __init__(self, val, left=None):
        self.val, self.left, self.right = val, left, None

n = 100000
# Build a chain: every node has only a left child (what sorted inserts produce).
root = None
for i in range(n):
    root = Node(i, root)
print("Skewed tree with", n, "nodes (each node has only a left child)")

# Our own stack lives on the heap, so depth is limited by memory, not by the call stack.
stack = [(root, 1)]
height = 0
while stack:
    cur, d = stack.pop()
    height = max(height, d)   # deepest node seen so far
    if cur.left:
        stack.append((cur.left, d + 1))
    if cur.right:
        stack.append((cur.right, d + 1))
print("height with an explicit stack =", height)
print("A recursive height() would need", n, "nested calls and can overflow the call stack")
# Time O(N), space O(h) on the heap.

followUps:
Generate many small random trees, run your code on each, and compare the result with a second, very simple solution that is obviously correct.

  1. Generator: build trees of 0 to about 20 nodes with random shapes; include empty, single-node, left-only and right-only chains, and duplicate values.
  2. Oracle: for a BST, mirror every operation in a sorted list or the library ordered set; for height or diameter, use a slow brute force.
  3. Invariants: after each operation check that inorder is sorted and the size is right.
  4. Reproduce: use a fixed random seed and print the failing tree, then shrink it.

Example: 10,000 rounds of random insert/delete on keys 0..9 against a TreeSet usually exposes a wrong two-children delete within seconds. Add one separate test with a 100,000-node chain for stack depth.

Store a tree in an array when its shape is complete or nearly complete, so there are no gaps: binary heaps and segment trees are the standard cases.

Put the root at index 0; the children of index i are at 2i + 1 and 2i + 2, and the parent is at (i - 1) / 2. No pointers are stored, so it uses less memory, and neighbours sit next to each other, which is fast for the CPU cache. The heap [1, 3, 2, 7, 4] means 1 -> (3 -> (7, 4), 2).

It is a poor choice for sparse or skewed trees: a chain of 20 right children would need index 220 - 2, about a million slots for 20 values. It also suits trees that keep being restructured by rotations badly, because whole subtrees would have to be moved; nodes with pointers are better there.
